units.citation: Herath et al. (2025). A Systematic Review of Forest Cover for Catchment‐Scale Flood Mitigation: A Nature‐Based Solution. Journal of Flood Risk Management.
units.quote:
Forest cover consistently impacts peak flow across catchments of all sizes, with a generalized linear rela-
tionship where the effect magnitude is approximately half the forest cover change. For example, a 20% increase in forest cover 
tends to reduce peak flow by 10% across small, medium, and large catchments.

relationship.outcome_raw: catchment peak flow change per change in forest cover (generalised linear relationship, effect about half the forest-cover change)

context.practice_as_described: forest cover change in catchments - afforestation, reforestation, woodlands and deforestation cases pooled
context.note: Mechanisms the review gives (p3): forests detain floodwater by infiltration, canopy interception and evapotranspiration, and reduce floodwater energy through surface roughness. Peak-flow evidence plotted in the pooled regressions is all from modelled scenarios (p6). Worked example in the abstract: a forest-cover increase of a fifth gives a peak-flow reduction of a tenth.

units.citation: Kimwanga et al. (2026). Who benefits from forest co-management? Heterogeneous welfare effects under rainfall shocks in Malawi. Trees, Forests and People.
units.quote:
Overall, VNRMC participation is 
associated with a 17.48% increase in forestry income and a 21.07 % in 
household non-forest income. Similarly, members of VNRMC have 3.2 
higher durable assets index and a 1.62% higher food consumption score 
than their counterparts non-participating members (Table 5).

relationship.outcome_raw: household food consumption score, VNRMC participants vs non-participants (pooled IPWRA ATT)

context.practice_as_described: household head is a member of a Village Natural Resource Management Committee (VNRMC) and engaged in forest co-management activities - 'a shared governance arrangement in which local communities and the state jointly manage forest resources'
context.note: Mechanism (p5): co-management 'grants communities' legal rights of access and sustainable use of forests, rights that can be translated into opportunities and income sources'; forest products act as a safety net during weather shocks. Forestry income = forestry wage labour, sales of wild fruits, mushrooms, insects, fauna, poles, timber, firewood. Cross-sectional survey of 743 households, 2023-2024 season; IPWRA ATT, PSM robustness. Reserves include two wildlife reserves (Majete, Vwaza Marsh). Pathway for food: wild foods collected from reserves (Fig. 3). Table 5: ATT 0.394, significant at 1%.

units.citation: Griscom et al. (2017). Natural climate solutions. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
units.quote:
Reforestation is the largest natural
pathway and deserves more attention to identify low-cost miti-
gation opportunities. Reforestation may involve trade-offs with
alternative land uses, can incur high costs of establishment, and
is more expensive than Avoided Forest Conversion (38). How-
ever, this conclusion from available marginal abatement cost
curves ignores opportunities to reduce costs, such as involving
the private sector in reforestation activities by establishing
plantations for an initial commercial harvest to facilitate natural
and assisted forest regeneration (39). The high uncertainty of
maximum reforestation mitigation potential with safeguards
(95% CI 2.7–17.9 PgCO2e y−1) is due to the large range in
existing constrained estimates of potential reforestation extent
(345–1,779 Mha) (14, 16, 40–42).

relationship.outcome_raw: maximum additional climate mitigation potential at the paper reference year, Reforestation pathway with food/fibre/biodiversity safeguards, global; confidence-interval bounds only (point estimate only in a figure bar and SI table, not in text)

context.practice_as_described: Griscom et al. 'Reforestation' pathway: conversion of non-forest to forest in forest ecoregions (main text p4 says the pathway includes new commercial plantations and plantation-facilitated natural and assisted regeneration), safeguarded: no reforestation of mapped cropland or of native non-forest ecosystems; boreal expansion excluded (albedo). BASELINE: business-as-usual land cover at 2030.
context.note: Global modelled potential M = A x F (extent x flux), extent from a geospatial analysis plus compiled published flux rates (Methods p5); the 95% CI 2.7-17.9 PgCO2e/yr reflects the range of constrained extent estimates 345-1,779 Mha (refs 14, 16, 40-42 = lineage, not independent evidence). Global aggregate, not per-ha: not comparable with plot-scale tCO2/ha/yr units. Point estimate (~10 PgCO2e/yr) is only in Fig. 1 bars / SI Table S1 - not quotable, not encoded. Pathway pools planting and regeneration -> cross_family. TNC-led (COI note). Modelled-only: engine caps class.

VNRMC participation and Rainfall shocks show that households 
participating in FCM through VNRMCs are have higher annual forestry 
income by 57% (Based on the difference of antilogs of 0.448 in Table 6), 
compared to non-participants. Conversely, VNRMC participation does 
not mitigate the effects of rainfall shocks’ on non-forestry income during 
the previous agricultural season. Despite the participation in VNRMC, 
the occurrence of rainfall shocks is likely to erode 36% of non-forestry 
income among smallholder households across forest reserves .

relationship.outcome_raw: annual NON-forestry income after a rainfall shock - participation does not protect it; shock still erodes non-forestry income among participants

context.practice_as_described: household head is a member of a Village Natural Resource Management Committee (VNRMC) and engaged in forest co-management activities - 'a shared governance arrangement in which local communities and the state jointly manage forest resources'
context.note: Mechanism (p5): co-management 'grants communities' legal rights of access and sustainable use of forests, rights that can be translated into opportunities and income sources'; forest products act as a safety net during weather shocks. Forestry income = forestry wage labour, sales of wild fruits, mushrooms, insects, fauna, poles, timber, firewood. Cross-sectional survey of 743 households, 2023-2024 season; IPWRA ATT, PSM robustness. Reserves include two wildlife reserves (Majete, Vwaza Marsh). Rainfall shock = SPI at or below minus one from 1981-2024 rainfall (methods define SPI below -0.79 as drought conditions); normal-condition ATT reported separately (Table 5). Table 6 interaction for non-forestry income is negative and significant at 5% (-0.311): coded as no protection (the authors' reading), not as a benefit.

units.citation: LAGANIÈRE et al. (2009). Carbon accumulation in agricultural soils after afforestation: a meta‐analysis. Global Change Biology.
units.quote: On average, afforestation resulted in an increase in SOC stocks of 26% for croplands, 3% for pastures, and o10% for natural grasslands; the two latter not being signiﬁcantly different from zero.

relationship.outcome_raw: change in SOC stock after afforestation of natural grassland (<10%, glyph o10%)

context.note: Meta-analysis (mixed linear model) of afforestation (plantation from seedlings/seeds) on agricultural or grassland soil; 'afforestation' excludes natural regeneration. income_group = modal (most sites high-income). Mean plantation age ~20-25 yr. Previous land use = natural grassland; "o10%" is a garbled "<10%" so no magnitude recorded; ns.; process: family re-homed active_planting -> plantation 2026-10-19 (Pete ruling 4, plantation split; audit pipeline/staging/plantation_audit/worklist.csv)
